content: The final decision-making process reassured all involved parties. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended non-clinical interventions to reduce unnecessary cesarean sections. Evidence from 14 studies showed no or minor methodological limitations in nine studies, while five studies had moderate to significant concerns. Minor concerns were noted regarding coherence, and moderate concerns were raised about adequacy. Data were collected from five world regions, including eight high-income countries (HICs), five middle-income countries (MICs), and one low-income country (LIC), with moderate confidence in the findings. Health professionals worldwide perceived maternity care systems as under-resourced in terms of both human and material resources. In settings where cesarean sections (CS) were a significant source of revenue, operating facilities were prioritized over laboring women's facilities, which were often poorly staffed and inadequate. Minor concerns were noted regarding coherence, and moderate concerns were raised about adequacy. Data from four world regions, predominantly HICs, were thin, with 10 studies showing no to moderate methodological limitations. Thick data were available from Iran, while thin data were collected from 13 countries. Coherence was high. Health professionals expressed concerns about high CS rates and associated morbidity across resource settings. In Iran and Tanzania, some professionals criticized colleagues who performed CS for non-medical reasons, viewing this as a violation of the ethical principle of do no harm. In European settings, interventions aimed at reducing unnecessary CS were more acceptable when shared within and between multidisciplinary groups. In countries like the United Kingdom, Denmark, Norway, and Sweden, organizations that successfully reduced CS rates fostered positive attitudes toward critical self-reflection, including audits, second opinions, and continuing medical education. Professionals acknowledged that reducing unnecessary CS was challenging but achievable and rewarding when respect, accountability, and shared responsibility supported women in achieving vaginal births. Minor concerns were noted regarding coherence, and moderate concerns were raised about adequacy. Thick data were available from three world regions, while thin data came from the African region (one study). Nine studies showed no to moderate methodological limitations, with thick data primarily from Europe. Only one study from the African region contributed to this finding, with high coherence. Some health professionals emphasized the importance of local opinion leaders endorsing projects. External facilitators were considered credible and culturally sensitive, understanding the challenges of specific practice settings. In some HICs, multidisciplinary teams included representatives from obstetrics, anesthesia, pediatrics, nursing, midwifery, allied health professionals, quality assurance, health records, and scheduling in secondary care. Moderate concerns were raised about coherence due to contradictions in available data. Major concerns were noted regarding adequacy, with thick data from one UK study. Data from four regions and across resource settings were thin, with low confidence. Six studies showed minor to significant methodological limitations, with thick data from one study. The extent of coherence was unclear. Dysfunctional teamwork within and between medical professionals, including the marginalization of midwives, was identified as a significant barrier to reducing unnecessary CS rates. Entrenched hierarchies in medicine, poor communication between maternity and theater staff, and strained relationships between obstetricians, midwives, and family doctors were frequently mentioned. Some midwives and obstetricians passionately criticized the marginalization of midwives, viewing their exclusion from birth as counterproductive. Seven studies showed no or minor methodological limitations, while four studies had moderate concerns. Moderate concerns were raised about adequacy, with thin data from eight studies and rich data from three studies across resource settings (United Kingdom, Iran, and Tanzania). Eleven studies showed minor to moderate methodological limitations, with thick data from across resource settings and high coherence. WHO recommendations for non-clinical interventions to reduce unnecessary CS targeted organizations, facilities, and systems. Resistance to change was rooted in the complexity of healthcare systems, with stakeholders reporting that CS rates were influenced by a complicated interplay of clinical and non-clinical factors. Moderate concerns were raised about coherence due to variations in reported complexity across papers. Major concerns were noted about adequacy, with few thick data (from one HIC) and thin data (from two MICs and five LICs). Data from 10 countries across five regions (Europe, Americas, Eastern Mediterranean, Western Pacific, and Africa) were included. Moderate concerns were raised about relevance, with five studies highly relevant and four moderately relevant to reducing unnecessary CS. Nine studies showed minor to moderate methodological limitations, with thin data across five regions and moderate coherence. In HICs and MICs, some stakeholders reported that the medicalization of childbirth devalued it as a physiological process. Interventionist organizational cultures limited opportunities for midwives and obstetricians to fulfill their roles optimally and for women to experience normal pregnancy and childbirth. Minor concerns were noted regarding coherence, with data similar within and across studies. Minor concerns were raised about adequacy, with thick data from four geographical regions, eight countries, five MICs, and three HICs. Thirteen studies showed no or minor methodological limitations, with thick data from four regions and high coherence. Studies were from MICs and HICs, with no LICs, leading to uncertain confidence in LICs. The value of human-to-human care during childbirth, including emotional labor, companionship, and advocacy, was highlighted. In HICs and one MIC, women appreciated labor support from doulas or midwives. Health professionals emphasized the importance of partner support and one-to-one midwifery or nursing care in HICs, where these were widely available. In MICs, labor support was recognized but limited by a shortage of midwives and inadequate facilities for partners to accompany women during labor. Eleven studies showed no or minor methodological limitations, while three had moderate concerns. Moderate concerns were raised about coherence, with some data similar within and across studies but variations explained by staff attitudes or unmet preferences of women. Minor to moderate concerns were noted about adequacy, with thick data from four regions, including HICs and MICs, but no LICs. Thirteen studies showed no to moderate methodological limitations, with thick data from four regions. Studies were from MICs and HICs, with no LICs, leading to uncertain confidence in LICs. Moderate coherence was observed. In HICs and MICs, some health professionals resisted change due to perceptions of women's preferences for obstetric-led care and CS. Some professionals also believed women lacked antenatal preparation for labor and vaginal birth. In Canada, the United Kingdom, and the United States, organizations promoting normal birth reported positive impacts on women's experiences. Fifteen studies showed no or minor methodological limitations, while four had moderate concerns. Minor concerns were noted regarding coherence, with data similar within and across studies. Minor concerns were raised about relevance, with 13 of 19 studies highly relevant. High confidence was observed, with 19 studies showing minor methodological limitations. Thick data were available from five regions, with high coherence and variations explained by degrees of concern. Studies were predominantly from MICs and HICs with high CS rates. Effective teamwork, communication, role demarcation, and respect across maternity care systems were identified as key components of successful multidisciplinary collaboration. Policymakers and practicing health professionals in HICs and MICs emphasized the importance of these factors in improving care quality and reducing unnecessary CS rates.
